title: America Is Closing Its Elementary Schools and Nobody Wants to Say Why
author: Anthony B. Bradley
source: Anthony B. Bradley on Substack (anthonybbradley.substack.com), May 18, 2026
summary: Anthony Bradley documents an accelerating wave of elementary-school closures moving quietly across the United States — San Jose closing five schools at once, districts across Texas, Georgia, Arizona, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and rural New England shuttering campuses, and 755 schools closing in a single recent year — all described in the neutral language of 'right-sizing' and 'under-enrollment.' Bradley argues these closures cannot be blamed on homeschooling or private schools: homeschooling stabilized at roughly 5–6% after its COVID spike, private enrollment has been flat at 9–10% for decades, and closures cluster precisely where private alternatives are least available. The actual cause, he contends, is a U.S. fertility rate near 1.6 births per woman — well below the 2.1 replacement level and declining since 2007 — which shrinks each cohort seven years before it reaches kindergarten. The elementary school, calibrated to the birth rate of seven years prior, is simply the first institution to register a society-wide retreat from family formation.
points: Closures are nationwide and bipartisan — blue and red states, urban and rural, wealthy and poor — with 755 schools closing in a single recent year and no sign of slowing.
The homeschooling explanation fails: it peaked near 9% in 2020–21 and has settled at 5–6%, far too small to account for a loss of 1.2–1.5 million public-school students since 2019.
Private schools aren't absorbing the missing children either — private enrollment has been flat at 9–10% for decades and by some measures is declining.
The geographic pattern refutes 'school flight': closures concentrate in low-income urban districts and rural counties where private alternatives barely exist.
The operative variable is demographic: a fertility rate around 1.6, below the 2.1 replacement level and falling since 2007, shrinks the cohorts schools are built on.
quotes: What they are not saying, at least not plainly, is that American families have stopped having enough children to fill the buildings their communities built for them.
Every district offers its own local explanation, but the underlying variable is the same in every zip code: there are not enough children.
The private sector is not absorbing the children that public schools are losing, because those children were never born.
The closures are everywhere because the cause is everywhere.
The United States fertility rate now sits at approximately 1.6 births per woman, well below the 2.1 replacement level required to maintain a stable population.
The elementary school is the first institution to feel demographic decline because children are the first demographic to disappear when a society stops forming families at a sustainable rate.
The buildings are closing. The question is whether anyone is willing to ask why.
